feedback: If a learner treats one effect (e.g. toppling) as the only sign of energy, show that distance pushed and loudness also grow with speed — all are evidence of more energy.
Reinforce naming: in each case the faster ball had more kinetic energy, shown by a bigger effect.
activities.intendedInsight: The relationship between speed and energy is general: it shows up in many kinds of evidence, not just one toppling task, so the explanation is about the moving object's energy rather than one specific effect.
learnerActions: Repeat the fast-vs-slow comparison but change what the ball hits: a sand crater to dent, a block to shove, or a buzzer/plate that sounds louder on a harder hit.
For each target, decide which speed produced the bigger effect and say what that tells you about the energy.
Compare across targets: check whether the same rule ('faster → more energy') shows up as more damage, more distance, AND a louder bang in your own results.
activities.title: Swap the evidence: same rule, different effect

feedback: A full response: more speed → more kinetic energy → more energy transferred to the dominoes (object held constant), and the child transfers the reasoning to a new case (e.g. where the energy went).
A partial response names more energy and more dominoes but can't connect it to energy TRANSFER, or slips into force or mass language — prompt gently toward 'what did the moving object hand over?'

A gap response explains only via 'more force/push' or claims a still object has kinetic energy — reteach the distinction between a contact push and carried energy, and that kinetic energy exists only while moving.
activities.intendedInsight: The reason matters: a speed→energy explanation predicts more effect because faster means more energy; the sameness of the object rules out mass, leaving speed as the cause, and a motionless object has no kinetic energy.
learnerActions: Roll the same object down a ramp from a low start, then from a high start (a higher start, on the same ramp, means it is moving faster at the bottom) into a row of dominoes/blocks.
BEFORE the fast roll, predict how many will move compared with the slow roll, AND say why.
Run the roll and compare your prediction with the result.
Answer the follow-ups: 'It's the same object both times — what does that let you rule out, so what's left?' and 'Where did the fast object's energy go after it hit?'
Consider a still object on the table that knocks nothing down: what does that say about whether a motionless object has kinetic energy?
activities.title: Predict-and-check: ramp roll into dominoes (diagnostic reasoning)
